title: Chamaeleon Infrared Nebula
caption: The Chamaeleon Infrared Nebula, imaged by the Gemini South telescope
credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA Acknowledgments: Image processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), J. Miller (Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: The Chamaeleon Infrared Nebula, as delicate as a butterfly's wing, was captured from Chile by the international Gemini Observatory. It lies close to the middle of the larger Chamaeleon I dark cloud, which ranks among the closest star-forming regions in the Milky Way.

Dark clouds are dense concentrations of cold gas and dust, and new stars form inside them when gravity pulls clumps of material together. Because the dust blocks much of their visible light, the young stars in such regions are often studied in infrared light, which passes through dust more easily.

Nebulae in star-forming regions can shine in different ways. Some glow because nearby stars energize their gas, while others become visible because dust reflects starlight toward us. This image was taken with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph on Gemini South through g, r, i and hydrogen-alpha filters. The Gemini Observatory is a Program of NSF NOIRLab.

understand.summary: Taken in visible light with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph on Gemini South through g, r, i and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The long exposure gathers far more light than the eye, bringing out faint, delicate structure in the nebula.

explore: The image was processed by T.A. Rector of the University of Alaska Anchorage, J. Miller of Gemini Observatory, and M. Zamani and D. de Martin of NSF NOIRLab. The Chamaeleon I dark cloud that surrounds it is itself a region where stars are forming.
